what_its_for: Pretomanid is an antibiotic used to treat a very serious type of tuberculosis (TB) called extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) or treatment-intolerant/nonresponsive multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB). It is always used together with two other TB medicines called bedaquiline and linezolid. It is not used alone and is not used for regular TB.
how_to_take: Take pretomanid by mouth with food. Swallow the tablet whole. Taking it with food helps your body absorb the medicine better and may reduce stomach upset. Always take it as part of the full 3-drug regimen your doctor prescribed. Do not stop taking it early, even if you feel better, unless your doctor tells you to stop.
dosing: The usual adult dose is one 200 mg tablet taken by mouth once a day with food for 26 weeks (about 6 months). Your doctor will tell you exactly how long to take it. Always take all three medicines (pretomanid, bedaquiline, and linezolid) together as directed.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is the same day you missed it. If you remember the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store pretomanid tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tablets in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect from moisture and heat. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not use tablets past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking pretomanid, as it can increase the risk of serious side effects on your heart and liver. Avoid taking pretomanid with certain medicines that affect heart rhythm without first talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, including herbal products. Do not take antacids or other medicines that contain aluminum or magnesium within a few hours of your dose without checking with your doctor.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: fast, slow, or irregular heartbeat or pounding in your chest; fainting or dizziness; yellowing of your skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); dark urine or severe stomach pain; vision changes or vision loss; numbness, tingling, or burning pain in your hands or feet; unusual tiredness or weakness; signs of low blood sugar (shakiness, sweating, confusion) if you have diabetes; or any new or worsening symptoms. Tell your doctor immediately if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
when_it_works: TB treatment takes a long time. You may start to feel better within the first few weeks, but it is very important to keep taking all your medicines for the full 26 weeks, even if you feel well. Stopping early can allow the TB bacteria to come back and become even harder to treat. Your doctor will do regular tests (blood tests, heart tests) to check that the medicine is working and that you are staying safe.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Pretomanid may harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and discuss this with their doctor. Breastfeeding: It is not known if pretomanid passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Pretomanid is not approved for use in patients under 18 years of age. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, tell your doctor before starting this medicine, as it can cause liver problems and your doctor will need to monitor you closely. Kidney problems: Dose adjustment is generally not needed for mild to moderate kidney problems, but tell your doctor about any kidney issues.
